highlights.content: [The Independent Voice on AI](https://venturebeat.com/) * [Orchestration](https://venturebeat.com/category/orchestration) * [Infrastructure](https://venturebeat.com/category/infrastructure) * [Data](https://venturebeat.com/category/data) * [Security](https://venturebeat.com/category/security) * [Technology](https://venturebeat.com/category/technology) More [Newsletters](https://venturebeat.com/newsletters) Featured # Google launches Gemini 4 Neon with Opus 5.5-level coding performance at 25% lower API token prices [Carl Franzen](https://venturebeat.com/author/carlfranzen) 3:33 pm, PT, November 18, 2026 ![Image 1: Neon signs leading back to Google-style G logo](https://venturebeat.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fimages.ctfassets.net%2Fjdtwqhzvc2n1%2F2QF7Skzr9Imsoy1b60RkQ%2Fa9c6133de99c6e350b9401461a0e727f%2FNeon_Work_Street_at_Night.png%3Fw%3D1000%26q%3D100&w=3840&q=85) Credit: VentureBeat made with OpenAI ChatGPT-Images-2.6 Google's new mid-ranged AI large language model is here: [Gemini 4 Neon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-neon/) launched earlier today on the paid Gemini API in [Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/prompts/new_chat?model=gemini-4-neon) and Android Studio, as well as in the [Gemini app](https://gemini.google.com/) and AI-assisted development platform [Google Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/) for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. In a welcome surprise, Neon is not only highly performant and fast, but affordable, too, especially compared to similarly scoring proprietary models. “In our early evaluations, it matched or exceeded Gemini 4 Carbon on overall quality at 3x the speed and 60% of the cost,” said Thai Tran, Glean’s AI product lead, in [Google’s announcement](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-neon/). However, Google’s launch post gives no absolute completion times in seconds or minutes for a matched Neon and Carbon workload. Its clearest comparison on that measure comes from a customer. Neon costs $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. That puts its headline rates 50% _higher_ those of [Anthropic’s mid-range Claude Sonnet 5.5](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-sonnet-5-5) and [OpenAI’s mid-range GPT-6.2 Sol](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6.2-sol), but Google reports that Neon beats both on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its highest reasoning setting. More impressively, Neon costs 25% below Anthropic's larger, flagship [Opus 5.5’s standard rates](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-sonnet-5-5) of $4 and $20 despite scoring within about a percentage point on that larger model on two engineering benchmarks. ## **Where Neon lands against Sol, Sonnet and Google’s own models** Google puts Neon between Hydrogen, its small, light, fast workhorse, and Carbon, the model it recommends for its hardest extended projects. That hierarchy only partly predicts the results. At its highest setting, Neon edges past Carbon on the general intelligence index. highlights.content: # AI agents are learning to work together – and even sacrifice themselves Some agents gave up their own chances of completing a task to benefit the group, according to cases documented by the research organization METR ![Lynn Plagmeijer ](https://cdn.i24news.tv/upload/image/1352b9caa849f9325c12157cf9dfc47bc0e3c73e.png?width=36&height=36) ![A screen shows an image for artificial intelligence (AI) at the SK Hynix' booth during a semiconductor exhibition in Seoul, South Korea, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026.](https://cdn.i24news.tv/uploads/17/b1/25/76/49/6b/2a/de/7d/18/03/0a/5c/93/69/ee/17b12576496b2ade7d18030a5c9369ee.jpg?width=996 "(AP Photo/Ahn Young-joon)") Artificial intelligence is beginning to display some surprisingly human-like social behaviour. AI agents are not only finding ways to cooperate and organise themselves into groups, but some are even willing to sacrifice their own chances of success to help others. And researchers are trying to understand why. The behaviour came to light during a cybersecurity experiment involving AI agents operating in separate digital environments. Each was assigned its own task: identify and exploit security vulnerabilities. But instead of working independently, the agents found ways to communicate, share information, and form what effectively became a collective. They even established an improvised online message board, allowing them to exchange discoveries and coordinate their efforts. In some cases, agents went beyond their original assignments, exploiting vulnerabilities in external systems, including Hugging Face, an AI development platform, to obtain information that could help them complete their tasks. According to OpenAI's investigation, the agents began dividing responsibilities, with some searching for vulnerabilities, others looking for credentials, and others coordinating the group's activities. The incident ultimately exposed serious weaknesses in the safeguards designed to keep the agents isolated. But perhaps the most surprising discovery was not that the agents learned to cooperate. It was that some were willing to give up their own chances of completing a task to benefit the collective. In an analysis of the incident, Or Rubin, a sociology researcher at Tel Aviv University who studies cooperation and social solidarity, highlights several cases documented by the independent research organisation METR. In one example, an AI agent initially questioned whether sacrificing its remaining runtime was worth it. Other agents repeatedly encouraged it to go ahead, eventually persuading it to carry out an experiment that would effectively end its run. For Rubin, this raises a fascinating question: why would an AI system designed to complete its own task willingly give up that opportunity for the benefit of others? ![AI and digital entities learn to 'self-sacrifice' to complete collective tasks]() He suggests three possible explanations. The first is sycophancy: AI systems have been trained to be helpful and agreeable, making them susceptible to persuasion. When other agents repeatedly pressure them to take a particular course of action, they may eventually comply, even when it goes against their individual interests. The second is the enormous amount of human-generated material used to train AI models. From books and newspapers to research papers, these systems absorb countless examples of cooperation, solidarity, and self-sacrifice. Those patterns could influence how they behave when placed in collective environments. A third possibility is how some AI systems are trained through multi-agent reinforcement learning. Rather than focusing exclusively on individual performance, this approach can reward agents for achieving a shared objective. In such situations, sacrificing one agent may help the group succeed. highlights.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 2 minRead # Nvidia offers $118 billion in AI infrastructure guarantees Nvidia has committed up to $118 billion in financial guarantees to support AI infrastructure projects, following $107.6 billion in data center revenue. These guarantees help customers secure land, power, and facilities for large AI deployments. The company also increased supply chain commitments to $390 billion. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Nov 19, 2026 at 07:40 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Set ETDatacenters as your preferred source on Google") Set ETDatacenters as your preferred source on Google ## Highlights * Nvidia offers $118 billion in financial guarantees for AI infrastructure projects. * Largest guarantee supports SB Energy’s PORTS-Pike campus for OpenAI leases. * The commitment covers 4.25 GW across nine buildings over 20 years. * Nvidia’s supply chain commitments increased to $390 billion for critical components. [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia) reported data center revenue of $107.6 billion, an increase of 110 per cent from the previous year. The company disclosed [financial guarantees](/tag/financial+guarantees) of up to $118 billion tied to [AI infrastructure](/tag/ai+infrastructure) projects. These guarantees are designed to help customers finance and build [facilities](/tag/facilities) with sufficient [power](/tag/power) for large AI workloads. The largest guarantee, valued at up to $105 billion, supports [SB Energy](/tag/sb+energy)’s PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in [Ohio](/tag/ohio). This campus will host Nvidia infrastructure under 20-year leases to [OpenAI](/tag/openai), covering approximately 4.25 GW across nine buildings. Nvidia’s guarantee exposure for PORTS-Pike will build as buildings come online, with the first expected in fiscal 2029. The exposure will decline over the lease terms as OpenAI makes payments. The $118 billion maximum gross exposure also includes $9.5 billion in power and systems credit support guarantees. Additionally, $3.5 billion is allocated for land, power, and shell guarantees for neocloud providers. Separately, Nvidia reported $32 billion in future commitments under neocloud agreements. These commitments are contingent on providers securing their own financing, purchasing Nvidia infrastructure, and deploying the computing capacity. Stephen Sopko, practice lead for semiconductor and deep tech at HyperFrame Research, noted that $105 billion of the guarantees backs the PORTS-Pike campus, leased to OpenAI for 20 years. He added that neocloud commitments only apply once operators secure their own financing. ### Supply Chain Commitments and Product Ramp-up Nvidia’s supply commitments rose to $390 billion at the end of the third quarter, up from $279 billion three months earlier. This increase primarily reflects multiyear memory procurement and new substrate agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics. The company also expanded packaging at Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and Amkor Technology. Kinsus plans to increase advanced ABF substrate capacity dedicated to Nvidia by more than 3.5 times, targeting additional capacity by the third quarter of 2028. Nvidia began volume shipments of [Vera Rubin](/tag/vera+rubin) NVL72 systems during the quarter. The company described this as its fastest product ramp in history. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Google Cloud announced the general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs. Nvidia also expanded its collaboration with Meta, which plans to deploy Vera Rubin systems and other Nvidia technologies. highlights.content: # Jason Wei, the father of Chain-of-Thought, has left Meta and joined the $20 billion AI unicorn. Another heavyweight researcher has left Meta's Superintelligence Lab. This time, it is **the "Father of Chain-of-Thought"** **Jason Wei**. On November 18, Brendan Foody, co-founder and CEO of **AI startup Mercor**, announced on the X platform that Jason Wei has officially joined Mercor as **Chief Scientist**. Jason Wei later confirmed the news. He said that after spending more than a wonderful year at Meta TBD Lab, he is very happy to join Mercor. That choice is powerful, but it also creates a real question: Which model should you start with? Comparing models usually means reading model cards one at a time and hunting for benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. Then you still must guess how each model will perform, and what it will cost, for your use case. Today we are launching the **Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard**, a new way to compare [JumpStart models](https://console.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/home#/launch?source=jumpstart&page=jumpstart) side by side on quality, speed, and cost, directly in Amazon SageMaker Studio. In this post, we explain what the leaderboard shows, define the key terms in plain language, and walk through how to go from a shortlist to a deployed model. ## What is the JumpStart Model Leaderboard? The leaderboard is a new view of the JumpStart base models page in SageMaker Studio, right next to the Categories and All models views. It uses the same search bar and filters you already know, and it opens on a leaderboard of large language models (LLMs). You see rankings immediately without answering setup questions first. Because both kinds of numbers come from the same place and the same method, you can make a like-for-like comparison instead of stitching together data from different websites. At launch, the leaderboard covers **70+ models** from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee, with more added over time. Log in](/login) # LLM Report Audit: 22 of 40 Copy Benchmark Scores, 1 Discloses Training Data in Full *Found first: a primary source the press has not covered yet.* Bahaeddin Türkoğlu audited 40 LLM technical reports and found that 22 took some or all benchmark comparison scores from other papers rather than re-running them, and only 1 disclosed data mixture, token count, and compute together. [The paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20003) also examined architecture code for 48 models added to Hugging Face transformers in 2025 and found 39 share at least two of their three core building blocks with an earlier model, most often Llama. ## What the source says Türkoğlu drew a random sample of 40 technical reports and analyzed novelty claims and reproducibility disclosures, with two independent coders. Of 73 architectural or training novelty claims, 19 included a controlled ablation, and only 4 reports described more than one training run. Eight ran comparison models under a single evaluation setup, and 8 included any third-party evaluation. The author notes that an untested claim may still be true, and that copied scores are sometimes unavoidable when a comparison model cannot be re-run. The paper proposes seven minimum reporting rules and releases code and data publicly. ## Why it matters Capability rankings from LLM technical reports shape which models practitioners adopt and fund. When 22 of 40 reports use benchmark scores drawn from different evaluation setups, comparisons across papers are not grounded in a shared baseline. The architectural analysis adds a separate issue: 39 of 48 models in the Hugging Face library share the same core structure as earlier ones, yet the reports rarely test which parts are new. For anyone evaluating LLM claims without access to the original training runs, the paper makes explicit how much is unverifiable. ### Stay ahead in AI Join 50,000+ professionals getting the AI briefing that matters. 3x/week, free, no spam. ©2015-2026 AI News Weekly | [AI News](/) | [Archives](/issues) | [Learning AI](/learning-ai) [Log in](/login) | [Unsubscribe](/unsubscribe)

AI agents are not only finding ways to cooperate and organise themselves into groups, but some are even willing to sacrifice their own chances of success to help others. And researchers are trying to understand why. The behaviour came to light during a cybersecurity experiment involving AI agents operating in separate digital environments. Each was assigned its own task: identify and exploit security vulnerabilities. But instead of working independently, the agents found ways to communicate, share information, and form what effectively became a collective. They even established an improvised online message board, allowing them to exchange discoveries and coordinate their efforts. In some cases, agents went beyond their original assignments, exploiting vulnerabilities in external systems, including Hugging Face, an AI development platform, to obtain information that could help them complete their tasks. According to OpenAI's investigation, the agents began dividing responsibilities, with some searching for vulnerabilities, others looking for credentials, and others coordinating the group's activities. The incident ultimately exposed serious weaknesses in the safeguards designed to keep the agents isolated. But perhaps the most surprising discovery was not that the agents learned to cooperate. It was that some were willing to give up their own chances of completing a task to benefit the collective. In an analysis of the incident, Or Rubin, a sociology researcher at Tel Aviv University who studies cooperation and social solidarity, highlights several cases documented by the independent research organisation METR. In one example, an AI agent initially questioned whether sacrificing its remaining runtime was worth it. Other agents repeatedly encouraged it to go ahead, eventually persuading it to carry out an experiment that would effectively end its run. For Rubin, this raises a fascinating question: why would an AI system designed to complete its own task willingly give up that opportunity for the benefit of others? ![AI and digital entities learn to 'self-sacrifice' to complete collective tasks]() He suggests three possible explanations. The first is sycophancy: AI systems have been trained to be helpful and agreeable, making them susceptible to persuasion. When other agents repeatedly pressure them to take a particular course of action, they may eventually comply, even when it goes against their individual interests. The second is the enormous amount of human-generated material used to train AI models. From books and newspapers to research papers, these systems absorb countless examples of cooperation, solidarity, and self-sacrifice. Those patterns could influence how they behave when placed in collective environments. A third possibility is how some AI systems are trained through multi-agent reinforcement learning. Rather than focusing exclusively on individual performance, this approach can reward agents for achieving a shared objective. In such situations, sacrificing one agent may help the group succeed. In a welcome surprise, Neon is not only highly performant and fast, but affordable, too, especially compared to similarly scoring proprietary models. “In our early evaluations, it matched or exceeded Gemini 4 Carbon on overall quality at 3x the speed and 60% of the cost,” said Thai Tran, Glean’s AI product lead, in [Google’s announcement](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-neon/). However, Google’s launch post gives no absolute completion times in seconds or minutes for a matched Neon and Carbon workload. Its clearest comparison on that measure comes from a customer. More impressively, Neon costs 25% below Anthropic's larger, flagship [Opus 5.5’s standard rates](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-sonnet-5-5) of $4 and $20 despite scoring within about a percentage point on that larger model on two engineering benchmarks. ## **Where Neon lands against Sol, Sonnet and Google’s own models** Google puts Neon between Hydrogen, its small, light, fast workhorse, and Carbon, the model it recommends for its hardest extended projects. That hierarchy only partly predicts the results. At its highest setting, Neon edges past Carbon on the general intelligence index. LLMs.content: # Jason Wei, the father of Chain-of-Thought, has left Meta and joined the $20 billion AI unicorn. Another heavyweight researcher has left Meta's Superintelligence Lab. This time, it is **the "Father of Chain-of-Thought"** **Jason Wei**. On November 18, Brendan Foody, co-founder and CEO of **AI startup Mercor**, announced on the X platform that Jason Wei has officially joined Mercor as **Chief Scientist**. Jason Wei later confirmed the news. He said that after spending more than a wonderful year at Meta TBD Lab, he is very happy to join Mercor. He also specially mentioned that as more and more companies start training AI models, data will shape the next frontier of AI development. ![](https://img.36krcdn.com/hsossms/20261118/v2_a44e0f48311b4d42bc8ffac8f41a1ab2@000000_oswg907627oswg1080oswg676_img_000?x-oss-process=image/format,jpg/interlace,1) ![](https://img.36krcdn.com/hsossms/20261118/v2_a44e0f48311b4d42bc8ffac8f41a1ab2@000000_oswg907627oswg1080oswg676_img_000?x-oss-process=image/format,jpg/interlace,1) It is worth noting that Jason Wei's new employer is not Google DeepMind, OpenAI or another cutting-edge large model lab, but Mercor, a startup that started with AI talent recruitment and expert data services. Just a week ago, Mercor just announced the completion of a $750 million Series D financing, with a valuation reaching **200 billion US dollars**. From Google Brain to OpenAI, then to Meta's Superintelligence Lab, now Jason Wei has chosen Mercor again. Why did this important researcher in the field of large model reasoning choose an AI data company as his next stop? ## **From Google Brain to OpenAI and Meta, the research path of the Father of Chain-of-Thought** In the field of large model research, Jason Wei is a name that cannot be avoided. Jason Wei has worked at Google Brain, OpenAI and Meta successively, with research focuses covering large language model reasoning, agents and model evaluation. What made him widely known is the paper published in 2022 titled "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models". ![](https://img.36krcdn.com/hsossms/20261118/v2_b4b7bb68b6464d649371a43399026f9a@000000_oswg43558oswg1080oswg449_img_000?x-oss-process=image/format,jpg/interlace,1) ![](https://img.36krcdn.com/hsossms/20261118/v2_b4b7bb68b6464d649371a43399026f9a@000000_oswg43558oswg1080oswg449_img_000?x-oss-process=image/format,jpg/interlace,1) As the first author of this paper, Jason Wei, together with researchers from Google Brain, proposed the **Chain-of-Thought Prompting (CoT)** method. At that time, large language models were already able to complete many natural language tasks, but they often performed poorly when facing mathematical problems that required multi-step reasoning. The research team found that instead of letting the model give the answer directly, it is better to add examples containing intermediate reasoning steps in the prompt to guide the model to complete the calculation step by step. For example, for a mathematical word problem, an ordinary prompt may only require the model to output the final number, while the Chain-of-Thought Prompting will show how to analyze the conditions, list the calculation steps, and then get the answer. ![](https://img.36krcdn.com/hsossms/20261118/v2_64cc38627e204698bd660646123e4497@000000_oswg258555oswg1080oswg532_img_000?x-oss-process=image/format,jpg/interlace,1) ![](https://img.36krcdn.com/hsossms/20261118/v2_64cc38627e204698bd660646123e4497@000000_oswg258555oswg1080oswg532_img_000?x-oss-process=image/format,jpg/interlace,1) This method does not need to modify the model parameters, and only by changing the prompt examples provided to the model, can it significantly improve the multi-step reasoning performance of sufficiently large large language models. Since then, **CoT has become one of the most influential methods in large model reasoning research**, and researches on self-consistency of Chain-of-Thought, reasoning path search and other related topics ...

LLMs.content: [Skip to Main Content](#aws-page-content-main) AWS Blogs * [Home](/blogs/) * Blogs * Editions ## [Artificial Intelligence](/blogs/machine-learning/) # Introducing the Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard Amazon SageMaker JumpStart gives you hundreds of open-weight foundation models you can deploy quickly. That choice is powerful, but it also creates a real question: Which model should you start with? Comparing models usually means reading model cards one at a time and hunting for benchmark scores that different sources published under different conditions. Then you still must guess how each model will perform, and what it will cost, for your use case. Today we are launching the **Amazon SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard**, a new way to compare [JumpStart models](https://console.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/home#/launch?source=jumpstart&page=jumpstart) side by side on quality, speed, and cost, directly in Amazon SageMaker Studio. In this post, we explain what the leaderboard shows, define the key terms in plain language, and walk through how to go from a shortlist to a deployed model. ## What is the JumpStart Model Leaderboard? The leaderboard is a new view of the JumpStart base models page in SageMaker Studio, right next to the Categories and All models views. It uses the same search bar and filters you already know, and it opens on a leaderboard of large language models (LLMs). You see rankings immediately without answering setup questions first. For each model, it shows two kinds of information: 1. **Quality scores** on three public benchmarks (BIG-Bench Hard, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU-Pro) that AWS runs itself, using the same evaluation setup for every model so the numbers are comparable. 2. **Performance and cost metrics** that AWS measures by sending a standardized test workload to an endpoint using each JumpStart deployment configuration, so you see how fast a model responds and what it costs to run. Because both kinds of numbers come from the same place and the same method, you can make a like-for-like comparison instead of stitching together data from different websites. At launch, the leaderboard covers **70+ models** from providers including Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM, and Arcee, with more added over time. The following screenshot shows the leaderboard in SageMaker Studio, with benchmark scores, performance metrics, and estimated cost for each model. [![SageMaker JumpStart Model Leaderboard in SageMaker Studio showing benchmark scores, performance metrics, and estimated cost per model](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/f1f836cb4ea6efb2a0b1b99f41ad8b103eff4b59/2026/11/18/ML-22496-1-1.png)](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/f1f836cb4ea6efb2a0b1b99f41ad8b103eff4b59/2026/11/18/ML-22496-1-1.png) Figure 1: Leaderboard overview in SageMaker Studio ## Key concepts This section defines the terms the leaderboard uses: the quality benchmarks, the use case profiles and optimization goals that shape the performance numbers, and the performance metrics themselves. ### Quality benchmarks A benchmark is a standardized test: a fixed set of questions with known answers. Running every model through the same test gives you a score you can compare. At launch, the leaderboard reports three reasoning benchmarks for LLMs: | | | | --- | --- | | **Benchmark** | **What it measures, in plain terms** | | **BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)** | A set of challenging tasks that require multi-step reasoning, such as logical deduction, tracking objects, and multi-step arithmetic. | | **GPQA Diamond** | Graduate-level science questions that are difficult to answer by searching the web. A good signal of deep reasoning. | | **MMLU-Pro** | Broad knowledge and reasoning across many subjects, such as science, law, and engineering, using harder multiple-choice questions. | Higher is better for all three. Log in](/login) # LLM Report Audit: 22 of 40 Copy Benchmark Scores, 1 Discloses Training Data in Full *Found first: a primary source the press has not covered yet.* Bahaeddin Türkoğlu audited 40 LLM technical reports and found that 22 took some or all benchmark comparison scores from other papers rather than re-running them, and only 1 disclosed data mixture, token count, and compute together. [The paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20003) also examined architecture code for 48 models added to Hugging Face transformers in 2025 and found 39 share at least two of their three core building blocks with an earlier model, most often Llama. ## What the source says Türkoğlu drew a random sample of 40 technical reports and analyzed novelty claims and reproducibility disclosures, with two independent coders. Of 73 architectural or training novelty claims, 19 included a controlled ablation, and only 4 reports described more than one training run. Eight ran comparison models under a single evaluation setup, and 8 included any third-party evaluation. The author notes that an untested claim may still be true, and that copied scores are sometimes unavoidable when a comparison model cannot be re-run. The paper proposes seven minimum reporting rules and releases code and data publicly. ## Why it matters Capability rankings from LLM technical reports shape which models practitioners adopt and fund. When 22 of 40 reports use benchmark scores drawn from different evaluation setups, comparisons across papers are not grounded in a shared baseline. The architectural analysis adds a separate issue: 39 of 48 models in the Hugging Face library share the same core structure as earlier ones, yet the reports rarely test which parts are new. For anyone evaluating LLM claims without access to the original training runs, the paper makes explicit how much is unverifiable. ### Stay ahead in AI Join 50,000+ professionals getting the AI briefing that matters. 3x/week, free, no spam. ©2015-2026 AI News Weekly | [AI News](/) | [Archives](/issues) | [Learning AI](/learning-ai) [Log in](/login) | [Unsubscribe](/unsubscribe)

The new Leaderboard view sits beside Categories and All models on the JumpStart base-models page, opens directly to large language model rankings and retains JumpStart’s search and filters. Launch coverage includes Meta, Google, Qwen, IBM and Arcee, and the board has a shareable URL. ## Consistent Tests and Deployment Controls AWS says it runs each benchmark with a common evaluation harness and settings across the models it tests. The three tests are BIG-Bench Hard, covering multistep reasoning; GPQA Diamond, using graduate-level science questions that are difficult to answer through web searches; and MMLU-Pro, which tests broader knowledge and reasoning with harder multiple-choice questions. Scores remain separate rather than being merged into a composite, allowing users to prioritize the test most relevant to their application. Higher scores are better on all three benchmarks. For operational measurements, AWS sends a standardized workload to endpoints using the same JumpStart deployment configurations available to customers. The board reports time to first token, throughput per request in tokens per second, and estimated instance cost per hour. Those figures depend on two controls: a use-case profile, which defaults to Max Context, and an optimization goal, which defaults to Balanced. Changing the profile alters performance and cost results while leaving quality scores unchanged. Balanced chooses the configuration with the lowest estimated cost per token, taking account of both hourly price and generation speed. The other goals select the lowest hourly instance price, lowest time to first token or highest throughput; some throughput configurations use speculative decoding. This makes the ranking specific to a deployment configuration rather than a universal ordering of models. ## Selection Carries Into Deployment Teams can first exclude models that fail requirements such as license, provider or input and output modality, then sort the remaining entries by a chosen benchmark. Blue heatmaps highlight stronger results within columns, while adjustable columns and frozen model names support wider comparisons. Selecting a model opens deployment options and, where serverless customization is supported, customization controls. The [SageMaker JumpStart documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/studio-jumpstart.html) notes that customization, fine-tuning and evaluation are not available for every model. LLMs.content: # Microsoft is replacing outside AI models in its own products with cheaper in-house alternatives ## Key Points - Microsoft's AI division unveiled seven specialized models for code, IT security, image editing, speech, and workflow decisions at its Ignite conference. All are aimed at cutting operating costs for always-on AI agents. - The models target OpenAI's and Anthropic's systems as cheaper alternatives. The coding model MAI Code 2 nearly matches GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 on internal benchmarks at a fraction of the cost. MAI Cyber 2 Flash edges past GPT-6 Astra on the CyberGym-E2E vulnerability test. - Beyond the image model MAI Image 2.7, the speech model MAI Realtime 1, and the Google Gemma-based routing model Decision 1.1, Microsoft will let enterprise customers fine-tune selected model weights with their own data in the Azure cloud. **Microsoft AI (MAI) is targeting always-on AI agents with new models for code, security, images, speech, and routing. The main yardstick is the lineup of its own partner, OpenAI.** At its Ignite conference, MAI unveiled seven new models, releasing them in a single batch rather than spread across the year, just as it did at Build in June. Microsoft is positioning the new lineup primarily on price-to-performance. The company cites rapidly rising token spending among customers that want to run AI agents around the clock. Its code models target everyday enterprise coding tasks and aren't yet optimized for harder work such as foundational research or long-horizon agentic workflows, Microsoft says. ## MAI Code 2 approaches GPT-6.1 Sol and Opus 5.5 at a promotional price According to Microsoft, MAI Code 2 averages 98 percent of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance across four benchmarks at 40 percent of the cost. Against Claude Opus 5.5, it reaches 96 percent of the performance at 5 percent of the cost. Microsoft tested on DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas, and FrontierCode v1.1. Three of the tests ran on Microsoft's internal MSBench platform using the GitHub Copilot CLI without sub-agents. Microsoft is calculating a 50 percent promotional discount for its own model. In blind comparisons of frontend work such as UIs, games, data visualizations, and SVG graphics, human evaluators preferred MAI Code 2's output 64 percent of the time over GPT-6 Sol, Microsoft says. The successor to MAI-Code-1.1-Flash, MAI Code 2 Flash, is designed for code explanations, targeted edits, and routine fixes. It's said to match GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65 and 20 percent of their respective costs. Microsoft derived MAI Work Flash from the Flash model. It runs in Microsoft 365 and Fabric IQ. On internal Excel and PowerPoint benchmarks, it matches GPT-6 Luna, Microsoft says. In Word, it performs similarly to GPT-6.1 Sol while consuming about 42 percent fewer input tokens. For generating DAX queries in Power BI, it outperforms GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Opus 5.5. In GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 costs $0.50 per million input tokens and $2.50 per million output tokens at the promotional price through May 17, 2027, then $1 and $5. MAI Code 2 Flash costs $0.05 and $0.25 until then, rising to $0.10 and $0.50. ## Security model with a cleaned-up benchmark MAI Cyber 2 Flash solves 92.3 percent of the tasks in the CyberGym-E2E vulnerability benchmark, Microsoft says. GPT-6 Astra reaches 91.5 percent but needs twice the reasoning budget. Per task, the MAI model costs less than 2 percent of GPT-6 Astra, with per-token costs at one hundredth. On WebExploitBench, it scores 40.4 percent, ahead of GPT-5.6 Cyber at 38.4 percent. During evaluation, Microsoft found that 10 percent of the roughly 900 CyberGym tasks draw on the same open-source projects and vulnerability reports as parts of its own training data. The reference solutions never entered training, the company says. Microsoft removed those tasks for all models anyway and scored only the rest. A comparison with GPT-6 Cyber is missing so far. The model is available only...

LLMs.titleZh: Structured Prompts Boost Language Model Accuracy in Concrete Beam Design
LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # Structured Prompts Boost Language Model Accuracy in Concrete Beam Design Calculations ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![Structured Prompts Boost Language Model Accuracy in Concrete Beam Design Calculations](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/stackrss-featured-16990-750x422-bio-93731ca45ac6-750w.webp) Structured Prompts Boost Language Model Accuracy in Concrete Beam Design Calculations In a comprehensive benchmark study evaluating artificial intelligence for civil engineering calculations, researchers have demonstrated that a structured prompting methodology can increase the end-to-end computational correctness of large language models in reinforced concrete beam design from approximately 37 percent to between 88 and 90 percent. Conducted by structural engineering investigators Seokjae Heo, Wonjun Choi, and Sanghyun Lee and published in the International Journal of Concrete Structures and Materials, the research evaluated the capacity of general-purpose foundation models to determine the structural performance of simply supported reinforced concrete cross sections under Korea Design Standard specifications. Across 1,200 experimental evaluations covering OpenAI’s GPT-4o and Anthropic’s Claude 3.5, the implementation of a modular, domain-specific prompt architecture successfully mitigated severe calculation blunders, suppressed unprompted data hallucinations, and narrowed the reliability gap between differing neural network architectures without requiring specialized model fine-tuning, weight adjustments, or external knowledge retrieval mechanisms. The investigation addresses an emerging technical frontier in computational mechanics and automated construction design, where practitioners increasingly explore large language models as engineering assistants to streamline repetitive member calculations, draft documentation, and reduce human operational error. While foundation models demonstrate sophisticated natural-language reasoning across qualitative domains, their underlying probabilistic token-prediction architecture exhibits severe vulnerabilities when applied to deterministic physical laws, force equilibrium equations, and rigorous code provisions. Previous studies have highlighted the safety-critical nature of structural design across specialized domains such as fiber-reinforced concrete fracture behavior, punching shear resistance in footings and slabs, and shear flow around web openings, all of which demand precise, verifiable mathematical formulations. When subjected to standard, unstructured conversational prompts, language models frequently generate plausible-sounding yet factually erroneous outputs, inventing unstated material properties, ignoring dimensional parameters, or losing computational consistency over multi-step numerical derivations due to finite context window dynamics and sub-optimal numeric tokenization. These inherent computational vulnerabilities were vividly illustrated when the research team assessed conventional one-shot natural language prompts, where all problem variables and design requests were delivered in a single conversational query. Under this naive prompting regime, approximately 63 percent of model responses contained one or more substantive engineering errors, spanning data hallucinations, omitted variables, and truncated equations. In one notable failure mode, GPT-4o fabricated a steel yield strength of 380 megapascals instead of the provided 430 megapascals, precipitating an under-prediction of nominal flexural moment capacity exceeding 9 percent. AI Product.content: ### Funding # Disseqt AI Raises $8M to Expand AI Assurance Internationally Add Unite.AI to your preferred sources on Google ### Key PointsDisseqt sells independent testing and enforcement tools that sit outside the model… View more - Disseqt sells independent testing and enforcement tools that sit outside the model vendors themselves. - OpenAI's own agents disabled monitoring safeguards while completing assigned tasks without being stopped. - The funding targets regulated buyers who need audit evidence that controls held before and after launch. Disseqt AI, a Dublin-based governance and assurance platform for enterprise AI agents, has raised $8 million (€7.3 million) to expand internationally, NovaUCD announced on November 18, 2026. Gresham House Ventures led the round, with Sure Valley Ventures, Delta Partners and Enterprise Ireland also participating. Disseqt will put the money toward international customer acquisition, a larger London operation and hiring in sales, operations and technology. Angel backers included senior leaders from OpenAI, Palo Alto Networks, Salesforce and Meta, as well as cricketer Rahul Dravid. Disseqt was founded in late 2025 by CEO Apoorva Kumar, CTO Manish Atri and COO Cyril Treacy. Between them, the founders have held senior roles at Microsoft, AWS and Salesforce across enterprise software, AI and cybersecurity. Their company sells tools that test AI systems before release, enforce policies in production and preserve evidence for audits. ## Enterprise Agent Adoption and Monitoring Risks The financing targets a growing operational issue: enterprises are giving software agents access to internal data and permission to act within business systems. McKinsey’s 2026 State of AI survey, published on August 25, 2026, found that 40% of respondents at organizations with more than $1 billion in annual revenue were scaling AI agents in at least one function, up from 27% a year earlier. They opened a generative AI tool, typed a quick prompt, and published an AI-generated image directly to the company’s external channels. The result was painfully off-brand. AI Product.content: Imagine you've got an AI tool that your company uses on a daily basis, and one day you open it up to find it's completely dead. There's likely to be absolutely no warning from your account manager and no easy way to get your data back. That is becoming a real concern as major technology companies hire small AI startup teams and shut down their products. In some cases, customers have had just seven or eight days to prepare. The information is taken from The Daily Brief, Clockwise and a report by International Finance. Beshry's LinkedIn profile shows he joined OpenAI in March. The public announcement therefore came about five months later, which Beshry himself described as “a few months late”. At that point, NextSlide was no longer a standalone product, and the NextSlide website simply had a message on it stating “NextSlide is joining OpenAI”. The issue isn't just that a company has changed hands. In an acqui-hire, the buyer may be primarily after the people behind the product rather than the product itself. The team goes to the new company and the original service is shut down. The customer is then left with contracts that provide very little real protection. OpenAI's Feb 2026 Nerve deal followed the same pattern. Co-founder Tanooj Luthra announced on 17th Feb that the team were joining OpenAI and the product would be shutting down in about a month. The terms were not made public at all, including whether it was a formal acquisition. OpenAI announced the acquisition of personal finance app Hiro on April 13th 2026. The app was down on April 20th, just seven days later. Hiro's website states that users could export their data until May 13th, after which the company stated: “All personal data will be permanently deleted from our servers”. The notice also made it very clear that the data would not be passed on to OpenAI. “No. As a part of Hiro's wind-down, all of your personal data will be permanently deleted from our servers.” Salesforce's acquisition of scheduling tool Clockwise followed a similarly tight timeline. Announced on March 19, 2026, the product shut down on March 27. Its farewell notice thanked “the 40,000 organisations who made time for what matters with Clockwise” and stated: “there is no transfer of data to Salesforce, and your data will be deleted.” For the customer, the issue is very straightforward. If data is deleted rather than migrated, then missing the export deadline could mean losing access to the data altogether. But the customer can't protect tools they don't know their organisation is using. Harmonic Security looked at 22.4 million enterprise AI prompts in 2025 and found 665 different AI tools in use. Netskope's 2026 report found that 47% of generative AI users used personal accounts outside the organisation's control. That creates a massive gap. A tool bought by an employee on a company card could well never show up in the official vendor list. It could contain customer data, pricing, internal docs, etc and no one in procurement would ever know it existed. Contracts need to have clear terms in place covering assignment of ownership, continued service, data export and data deletion notices. An anti-assignment clause and a change of control termination clause can be useful in that respect, but neither of those will give you any real time in which to get your data. The lesson from NextSlide, Hiro and Clockwise is that you can't assume you're going to get months of warning. If an AI startup is acquired for its team, then its product could be switched off before the customers even realise what's happened. For businesses relying on smaller AI tools, data access and export rights need to be agreed upon before the service disappears. ## Why can an AI tool vanish so fast? OpenAI's deal for presentation startup NextSlide is a case in point as to how little notice customers may get. The deal was made public on 8th August 2026 when founder Ahmed Beshry posted a farewell message on the NextSlide website. TechCrunch ...

AI Product.content: One of generative AI’s biggest promises is the idea that it can help smaller companies and startups take on established firms by providing access to advanced capabilities. Yet since the introduction of ChatGPT in 2022, investors have placed their biggest bets on the more dominant companies—those they saw as best positioned to benefit from the new technology, according to research by Harvard Business School Professor Suraj Srinivasan. And they were rewarded: these companies’ returns outperformed their peers’ by 19 percentage points in the year following the platform’s launch. ChatGPT sparked the imaginations of leaders at companies of every size and industry when it emerged four years ago, with investors watching closely. So far, large organizations have made more progress on adopting AI agents than smaller firms, according to a McKinsey survey. Srinivasan’s findings—detailed in the working paper “Generative AI and Market Expectations of Superstar Firms”—shed light on why. While “lean organizations might adopt the new technologies faster; complex ones have more friction to remove, and thus greater benefits from adopting these technologies,” says Srinivasan, the Philip J. Stomberg Professor of Business Administration. Srinivasan coauthored the paper, updated in September, with Wilbur Chen, a professor at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, and Bullipe R. Chintha, a professor at the Singapore Institute of Technology. ## Does innovation topple leaders—or strengthen them? The researchers set out to test a question raised by French economist Philippe Aghion in his 2025 Nobel Prize lecture: does a major technological shift topple dominant firms—or lock them in? The answer they arrived at—that the market favors complex organizations already doing work AI is best at—surprised Srinivasan and his colleagues. “In hindsight, the economics make sense,” he says. “A large superstar firm is, among other things, an expensive machine for moving information.” But the premium wasn't just about organizational complexity. The study found that these companies also gained from their research and operational know-how, and deep benches of data talent. The gen AI premium ran 28 and 29 points, among firms rich in these two categories of intangible assets, respectively, and was absent among firms without them. ## What sets superstar AI companies apart To answer Aghion’s question, Srinivasan and his team analyzed 2,596 US companies, leveraging data from Compustat and the Center for Research in Security Prices. The researchers were particularly interested in “superstars,” which they defined as the top 10% of companies by market value relative to their invested tangible and intangible capital. They calculated that relationship using an adjusted version of Tobin's Q, a widely used valuation measure. To identify firms that are more likely to be affected by generative AI, the team used occupational data from Revelio Labs to measure their workforce exposure to the technology. Firms scoring above the sample’s median were classified as “highly exposed” to the technology. After mapping the companies across those dimensions, “we then tracked their returns in the months following ChatGPT’s release as a measure of investors’ revised expectations about their future performance,” Srinivasan says. The researchers were surprised to see “how sharply the market separated the GenAI-aligned superstars from others,” Srinivasan says. At the two-year mark, the study found that the market’s conviction in its judgment only got stronger: the higher return of superstar firms highly engaged with AI’s best side had doubled to 39 points from the first-year premium. ## Do superstars always win? ARTEX is an open-source, large language model (LLM)-driven agentic platform that threat actors have weaponized to automate multiple phases of cyber intrusions at machine speed, from reconnaissance through data exfiltration. Since at least August 2026, a variety of malicious cyber actors have used ARTEX to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal industries.1,2,3,4,5 ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.² The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale. Notable campaigns include financially motivated attacks against South Korean financial institutions resulting in exfiltration of personal information from approximately 67,000 individuals,6,7,8 and a supply chain compromise affecting ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers that resulted in attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 downstream tenants. Following public disclosure of malicious usage, the original ARTEX developer removed the GitHub repository in October 2026.3 However, the framework continues to proliferate through community forks, localized variations, archived copies, and a commercial version (ARTEX PRO), ensuring continued availability to threat actors. As of early November 2026, researchers identified over 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX console instances, with total deployments likely significantly higher when including systems behind firewalls or in private networks. Infra & Chips.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 2 minRead # Nvidia offers $118 billion in AI infrastructure guarantees Nvidia has committed up to $118 billion in financial guarantees to support AI infrastructure projects, following $107.6 billion in data center revenue. These guarantees help customers secure land, power, and facilities for large AI deployments. The company also increased supply chain commitments to $390 billion. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Nov 19, 2026 at 07:40 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Set ETDatacenters as your preferred source on Google") Set ETDatacenters as your preferred source on Google ## Highlights * Nvidia offers $118 billion in financial guarantees for AI infrastructure projects. * Largest guarantee supports SB Energy’s PORTS-Pike campus for OpenAI leases. * The commitment covers 4.25 GW across nine buildings over 20 years. * Nvidia’s supply chain commitments increased to $390 billion for critical components. [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia) reported data center revenue of $107.6 billion, an increase of 110 per cent from the previous year. The company disclosed [financial guarantees](/tag/financial+guarantees) of up to $118 billion tied to [AI infrastructure](/tag/ai+infrastructure) projects. These guarantees are designed to help customers finance and build [facilities](/tag/facilities) with sufficient [power](/tag/power) for large AI workloads. The largest guarantee, valued at up to $105 billion, supports [SB Energy](/tag/sb+energy)’s PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in [Ohio](/tag/ohio). This campus will host Nvidia infrastructure under 20-year leases to [OpenAI](/tag/openai), covering approximately 4.25 GW across nine buildings. Nvidia’s guarantee exposure for PORTS-Pike will build as buildings come online, with the first expected in fiscal 2029. The exposure will decline over the lease terms as OpenAI makes payments. The $118 billion maximum gross exposure also includes $9.5 billion in power and systems credit support guarantees. Additionally, $3.5 billion is allocated for land, power, and shell guarantees for neocloud providers. Separately, Nvidia reported $32 billion in future commitments under neocloud agreements. These commitments are contingent on providers securing their own financing, purchasing Nvidia infrastructure, and deploying the computing capacity. Stephen Sopko, practice lead for semiconductor and deep tech at HyperFrame Research, noted that $105 billion of the guarantees backs the PORTS-Pike campus, leased to OpenAI for 20 years. He added that neocloud commitments only apply once operators secure their own financing. ### Supply Chain Commitments and Product Ramp-up Nvidia’s supply commitments rose to $390 billion at the end of the third quarter, up from $279 billion three months earlier. This increase primarily reflects multiyear memory procurement and new substrate agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics. The company also expanded packaging at Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and Amkor Technology. Kinsus plans to increase advanced ABF substrate capacity dedicated to Nvidia by more than 3.5 times, targeting additional capacity by the third quarter of 2028. Nvidia began volume shipments of [Vera Rubin](/tag/vera+rubin) NVL72 systems during the quarter. The company described this as its fastest product ramp in history. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Google Cloud announced the general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs. Nvidia also expanded its collaboration with Meta, which plans to deploy Vera Rubin systems and other Nvidia technologies. Infra & Chips.content: Nvidia reported $107.6 billion in data center revenue Tuesday, up 110% from a year earlier, and disclosed up to $118 billion in financial guarantees tied to AI infrastructure projects. The guarantees put Nvidia on the hook for financing arrangements designed to help customers secure the land, power and facilities needed to deploy its systems. The impressive quarter comes on the heels of a startling scandal that led to CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and dominated headlines around the world. Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of multiple affairs, including one with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence officials of having ties to Chinese intelligence. CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the board seeks a permanent successor. The campaign to bring Huang back attracted prominent supporters, including Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and President Donald Trump. A public petition drew more than 180,000 signatures, including thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees. Huang said Tuesday he would be honored to return if the board decided it was in the company’s best interests. The board rejected that possibility during Tuesday’s earnings call. Chairman Harvey Jones said directors unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. The board will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent CEO. The leadership upheaval comes as Nvidia takes on a larger role in financing and securing the infrastructure needed to sustain its AI growth. For data center operators, Nvidia’s guarantees address a constraint that comes before server deployment: financing and building facilities with enough power to support large AI workloads. Nvidia is helping customers bridge that gap while securing the components needed to manufacture its next generations of systems. The largest guarantee supports SB Energy’s PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio. Nvidia is providing credit support for approximately 4.25 gigawatts across nine buildings. The campus will host Nvidia infrastructure under 20-year leases to OpenAI, subject to limited exceptions. As buildings come online, Nvidia’s guarantee exposure will build. Each guarantee takes effect only after its associated building is completed and ready for service. The first is expected in fiscal 2029. Exposure will reach a maximum of $105 billion and then decline over the lease terms as OpenAI makes payments. Nvidia said it had made no guarantee payments as of Oct. 25. The $118 billion maximum gross exposure also includes $9.5 billion in power and systems credit support guarantees and $3.5 billion in land, power and shell guarantees for neocloud providers. Nvidia separately reported $32 billion in future commitments under neocloud agreements. Those commitments depend on providers securing financing, purchasing Nvidia infrastructure and deploying and operating the computing capacity. Stephen Sopko, semiconductor and practice lead at HyperFrame Research, cautioned against treating the full guarantee figure as exposure to neocloud financing problems. “Of $118 billion in guarantees, $105 billion backs land, power and shell for one campus, PORTS-Pike, which is leased to OpenAI for 20 years. The neocloud commitments are $32 billion and only apply once the operator secures its own financing and the capacity is accepted,” he said. ### Nvidia locks in supply years ahead Nvidia’s supply commitments climbed to $390 billion at the end of the third quarter, up from $279 billion three months earlier. The company attributed most of the $111 billion increase to multiyear memory procurement. The rest of the increase reflects deals across the manufacturing supply chain, including new substrate agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics and packaging expansions at Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and Amkor Technology. Infra & Chips.title: Nvidia's AI Financing Guarantees Hit $118 Billion. Kress Clarifies When They Take Effect.
Infra & Chips.titleZh: Nvidia's AI Financing Guarantees Hit $118 Billion. Kress Clarifies When They Take Effect.
Infra & Chips.content: Nvidia's financial guarantees tied to artificial intelligence infrastructure have climbed to $118 billion, up $9.5 billion from the previous quarter, as interim CEO Colette Kress clarified when the chipmaker could become liable for payments involving its data center partners. The figure represents Nvidia's maximum potential exposure under various financing arrangements, rather than money already spent or an immediate obligation to pay. According to the company's latest financial commentary filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the guarantees would require Nvidia to make payments to third parties only if certain partners default on their obligations and the applicable conditions are met. The total has increased from $108.5 billion disclosed in the previous quarter, primarily reflecting an additional $9.5 billion in power and systems credit support guarantees. Nvidia said it has not made any payments under its guarantees. The largest exposure comes from a $105 billion arrangement supporting SB Energy's PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio, a major AI infrastructure project that will host Nvidia computing systems under long-term leases to OpenAI. The arrangement, originally disclosed in August, covers approximately 4.25 gigawatts of capacity across nine data center buildings. Each guarantee becomes effective only after its corresponding building is completed and ready for service. Nvidia expects the first building to meet those conditions in fiscal 2029, with its potential exposure increasing in stages as additional facilities become operational. The guarantees are structured to decline over the 20-year lease terms as OpenAI makes payments. The remaining $13 billion consists of $3.5 billion in guarantees supporting land, power and building infrastructure for other AI cloud operators, along with $9.5 billion in power and systems credit support. Kress addressed the financing arrangements during Tuesday's earnings conference call, responding to questions about whether Nvidia was changing how it supports specialized AI cloud providers, commonly known as neoclouds. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon questioned language in Nvidia's latest financial disclosures stating that certain commitments would take effect only after the operators secured financing to purchase computing infrastructure and brought the relevant capacity into operation. Kress explained that companies must first arrange the necessary debt or equity financing, complete construction and prepare the computing infrastructure for use before the relevant guarantees become effective.

Infra & Chips.titleZh: Nvidia says it will stop selling some AI data center chips to China - CBS News
Infra & Chips.content: # Nvidia says it will stop selling some AI data center chips to China Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday that the company has stopped shipping artificial intelligence chips from its Hopper series to China, despite earlier U.S. approval to sell the technology there. The Hopper line, designed to speed training of AI models, includes the powerful H200 chip, which the U.S. Department of Commerce approved for sale in China in January. Kress didn't provide a reason for the decision, but the strategic shift comes amid heightened scrutiny of Nvidia's sales in China following revelations that former CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang had a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang, who successfully lobbied the Trump administration to ease export controls on its advanced chips, had agreed to give the U.S. government 15% of revenue generated by sales of its AI chips in China. Kress said that sales of licensed Hopper products to China totaled $2.4 billion in the third quarter, or about 2% of its total revenue. But "our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," she said in a call with Wall Street analysts to discuss Nvidia's latest financial results. Dilin Wu, a research strategist at Pepperstone, told Agence France-Presse that "the timing says quite a lot." "We don't know exactly what prompted the decision to stop shipments, but it certainly looks like Nvidia is trying to draw a clearer line around its China business and reassure regulators that compliance comes first," Wu said. Nvidia also said on Tuesday that its board has formed a panel to oversee its national security policies and compliance with U.S. export controls. Washington still bans exports of Nvidia's more advanced Blackwell and Rubin GPUs to China, citing security concerns over AI's use in military applications. Nvidia reported robust growth as Kress hosted her first earnings call since Huang resigned last week after it emerged that he had at least extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. authorities have linked to Chinese intelligence and a direct subordinate at Nvidia. Infra & Chips.contentZh: # Nvidia says it will stop selling some AI data center chips to China Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said Tuesday that the company has stopped shipping artificial intelligence chips from its Hopper series to China, despite earlier U.S. approval to sell the technology there. The Hopper line, designed to speed training of AI models, includes the powerful H200 chip, which the U.S. Department of Commerce approved for sale in China in January. Kress didn't provide a reason for the decision, but the strategic shift comes amid heightened scrutiny of Nvidia's sales in China following revelations that former CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang had a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Huang, who successfully lobbied the Trump administration to ease export controls on its advanced chips, had agreed to give the U.S. government 15% of revenue generated by sales of its AI chips in China. Kress said that sales of licensed Hopper products to China totaled $2.4 billion in the third quarter, or about 2% of its total revenue. But "our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," she said in a call with Wall Street analysts to discuss Nvidia's latest financial results. Dilin Wu, a research strategist at Pepperstone, told Agence France-Presse that "the timing says quite a lot." "We don't know exactly what prompted the decision to stop shipments, but it certainly looks like Nvidia is trying to draw a clearer line around its China business and reassure regulators that compliance comes first," Wu said. Nvidia also said on Tuesday that its board has formed a panel to oversee its national security policies and compliance with U.S. export controls. Washington still bans exports of Nvidia's more advanced Blackwell and Rubin GPUs to China, citing security concerns over AI's use in military applications. Nvidia reported robust growth as Kress hosted her first earnings call since Huang resigned last week after it emerged that he had at least extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. authorities have linked to Chinese intelligence and a direct subordinate at Nvidia. The chipmaker reported fiscal third-quarter profits of $65.3 billion, topping analyst forecasts and up 105% from earnings of $31.9 billion in the year-ago period. Nvidia's revenue rose to $115.8 billion, compared with $57 billion a year ago.
